title: Why Do Farts Smell So Bad? The Secret Is Brewing in Your Gut
summary:
Why do farts smell so bad? That question came from Daisy, age 7, of New York. A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day, the source says -- enough gas, added up, to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. They help break down food your stomach cannot handle on its own. As they work, they act like mini chemical factories, releasing nutrients and waste gases. Those gases mix with air you swallow, then burst out as farts.

Most of a fart is odorless gas, like the air we breathe. Between 20% and 90% of its volume is nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% is oxygen, up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane.

The stink comes from tiny amounts of gases that contain sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell alone, but with other elements it makes molecules that reek. One culprit is hydrogen sulfide, famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Another is methanethiol, which can smell like cabbage, sewage, or skunk spray. Just one molecule of hydrogen sulfide among a million other gas molecules is enough to do the job.

What you eat shapes the smell. High-fiber foods like beans and grains can make farts bigger and louder. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur. They are plentiful in meat, dairy, and eggs, and found to a lesser degree in beans and grains. Cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower also contain sulfur molecules.

The loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It is the sulfur that packs the smelly punch. Farting is also useful: it relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.
why_it_matters: Understanding your gut helps you understand your own body: what you eat changes the microbes inside you, and those tiny organisms affect how you feel every day.
